statement: Prove that the open balls of a metric space form a basis for a topology.
solution: Every point x lies in B(x,1), so the balls cover X. If z∈B(x,r)∩B(y,s), let t=min(r-d(x,z), s-d(y,z))>0; the triangle inequality gives B(z,t)⊆B(x,r)∩B(y,s). These two conditions are exactly the basis criterion, so the balls form a basis.

statement: Prove that every metric space is first countable.
solution: At each point x, the balls B(x,1/n) for n∈N form a countable neighborhood basis: any open U∋x contains some B(x,ε), and choosing n>1/ε gives B(x,1/n)⊆B(x,ε)⊆U. Hence X is first countable.

statement: Prove that a subspace of a metric space is metrizable by the restricted metric.
solution: Let (X,d) be metric and A⊆X. The restriction d|A×A is a metric on A. Its balls are B_A(a,r)=A∩B_X(a,r), which are exactly the intersections of X-balls with A; these generate the subspace topology on A. Hence the subspace topology is induced by d|A.

statement: Prove that a function f: X → Y between metric spaces is continuous at x0 in the topological sense if and only if the epsilon-delta condition holds.
solution: (topological ⇒ ε-δ) Given ε>0, B(f(x0),ε) is open; f^{-1} of it is open and contains x0, so it contains some B(x0,δ), i.e. d(x,x0)<δ ⇒ d(f(x),f(x0))<ε. (ε-δ ⇒ topological) For open V∋f(x0), pick ε with B(f(x0),ε)⊆V, then δ from the condition gives f(B(x0,δ))⊆V, so f^{-1}(V) is a neighborhood of x0.

statement: Prove that every convergent sequence in a metric space is Cauchy.
solution: If x_n→x, then given ε>0 there is N with d(x_n,x)<ε/2 for n≥N. For m,n≥N, d(x_m,x_n)≤d(x_m,x)+d(x,x_n)<ε by the triangle inequality. Hence (x_n) is Cauchy.

statement: Prove that the distance-to-a-set function x ↦ d(x, A) is continuous, in fact 1-Lipschitz.
solution: For any a∈A, d(x,A)≤d(x,a)≤d(x,y)+d(y,a); taking inf over a gives d(x,A)≤d(x,y)+d(y,A), so d(x,A)-d(y,A)≤d(x,y). By symmetry |d(x,A)-d(y,A)|≤d(x,y), i.e. the map is 1-Lipschitz, hence continuous.

statement: Prove that the metric d: X × X → R is continuous, where X × X carries the product topology.
solution: By the reverse triangle inequality, |d(x,y)-d(x',y')|≤d(x,x')+d(y,y'). Given ε>0, if d(x,x')<ε/2 and d(y,y')<ε/2 then |d(x,y)-d(x',y')|<ε. Since basic neighborhoods in X×X are products of balls, d is continuous.

statement: Prove that the bounded metric d'(x,y) = min(d(x,y), 1) induces the same topology as d.
solution: For r≤1 the d'-ball and d-ball of radius r coincide, and every topology-defining requirement only needs small balls. Since for r<1, B_{d'}(x,r)=B_d(x,r), each metric's small balls are the other's, so they have the same basis of small balls and hence the same topology.

statement: Prove that a compact metric space is separable.
solution: For each n, the balls B(x,1/n) cover X; by compactness pick a finite subcover with centers F_n. Let D=∪_n F_n, a countable set. Any point x and ε>0: choose n>1/ε, then x∈B(c,1/n) for some c∈F_n, so d(x,c)<ε. Hence D is dense and X is separable.

statement: Prove that a compact metric space is second countable.
solution: A compact metric space is separable (m09) with countable dense set D. The balls {B(d,q) : d∈D, q∈Q+} form a countable family; one checks they are a basis (given open U∋x, pick a ball around x inside U, then a nearby center in D and rational radius). A separable metric space is second countable.

statement: Prove that a uniformly continuous function is continuous.
solution: Uniform continuity gives, for each ε>0, a single δ>0 with d(x,y)<δ ⇒ d(f(x),f(y))<ε for all x,y. In particular this δ works at each fixed x0, which is the ε-δ definition of continuity at x0. So f is continuous everywhere.

statement: Prove that two metrics d1, d2 on X generate the same topology if each ball of one contains a ball of the other around the same point.
solution: The condition says: for every x and every d1-ball around x there is a d2-ball around x inside it, and vice versa. This means every d1-open set is d2-open and conversely (using b11-style local basis containment). Hence the two topologies coincide.

statement: Prove that a closed subset of a complete metric space is complete.
solution: Let F be closed in complete X and (x_n) Cauchy in F. It is Cauchy in X, so converges to some x∈X. Since F is closed and contains all x_n, the limit x∈F. Hence every Cauchy sequence in F converges in F, so F is complete.

statement: Prove that an isometry between metric spaces is a homeomorphism onto its image.
solution: An isometry f satisfies d(f(x),f(y))=d(x,y), so it is injective and maps balls to balls: f(B(x,r))=B(f(x),r)∩f(X). Thus f and f^{-1} (on the image) are continuous, and f is a bijection onto its image, hence a homeomorphism onto f(X).

statement: State the Banach fixed-point theorem and identify the hypotheses it needs.
solution: Banach fixed-point theorem: if (X,d) is a nonempty complete metric space and T:X→X is a contraction (d(Tx,Ty)≤k d(x,y) for a constant k<1), then T has a unique fixed point, and iterating T from any starting point converges to it. The essential hypotheses are completeness of X and the strict contraction constant k<1.

statement: Prove that in a metric space a set is closed if and only if it is sequentially closed.
solution: Metric spaces are first countable, so closure equals sequential closure (s15). A set F is closed iff F=cl(F) iff F contains the limit of every convergent sequence of its points, i.e. iff F is sequentially closed.
